item.title: index
item.description:
For LLMs: Start here. Navigate to a directory index for scoped exploration, or jump directly to a core document below. For Humans: See above… but use the graph to guide your exploration! BACKLOG.kanban is a good place to see where you can help :) We don't log data just to have data.
We log coffee (`pour coffee`) because we are chasing the perfect extraction, and we want to remember how that Ethiopian light roast tasted at a 1:15 ratio.We log music (pour music) because the energy of a live set and the people we shared it with are memories worth keeping.
We log ourselves (`pour me`) because our passing thoughts, midnight epiphanies, and daily anxieties deserve a place to rest outside our own heads.We want to write more about the things that bring us joy. To do that, the tool must get out of the way entirely..obsidian/ is vault configuration and snippet state, not part of the documentation corpus.
pour-design-spec — Complete design specification (source of truth)
the_pour_manifesto — Why we build Pour
System-Architecture-Overview — Concise subsystem map
pour-preset-hierarchy — Preset hierarchy drilldown spec (TUI picker, preset_axes, ungrouped, validation)
v0.2.0-Foundation — Capture-loop foundation (shipped)
v1.0.0-Release — Aspirational freeze criteria Pour is not a workspace. It is a reflex.
It is a capture tool that meets you where you already are — terminal at the desk, PWA in your pocket — designed to be as fluid and instantaneous as the gesture that invokes it.
Velocity is a Feature: The time between having a thought and executing the capture must be near zero. pour lives where you already are — your terminal at the desk, your phone in the wild — and is just the tool you need at the moment you need it. No cold-start app launch, no folder to find, no schema to format by hand. The phone surface costs more friction than the terminal; that cost is worth paying when the alternative is forgetting the thought entirely. See Capture-Reflex.
Capture First, Synthesize Later: pour separates the act of recording from the act of organizing. You pour the raw data into the vault flawlessly formatted. You can open Obsidian on Sunday to make sense of it all.
Plaintext is Forever: We reject proprietary databases. A memory should not be locked behind a subscription or a specific app version. Everything pour generates is strict, portable Markdown and YAML — see field-types for the full vocabulary. It belongs to you. Fluidity: The name is the instruction. You don't "execute a script" or "insert a database row." You pour a V60. You pour your thoughts. Type the verb at the desk, drag the gesture in your pocket — the act is the same. It is a continuous, natural motion. cargo build # compile cargo run # run dashboard cargo run -- coffee # run a specific module cargo test # run all tests cargo clippy # lint cargo fmt # format
Pour writes to Obsidian via a __hybrid transport layer__:
API — HTTPS via reqwest to Obsidian Local REST API (https://127.0.0.1:27124, accepts self-signed certs)
File System — Direct std::fs fallback if API unavailable. In append mode, this fallback materialises as an atomic timestamped note rather than a destructive in-place write.
API query -> disk scan -> ~/.pour/cache/state.json cache -> freetext input. Novel values entered into `dynamic_select` fields trigger inline note creation back into the vault.Last Updated: 2026-04-29 Documentation Version: v0.1.0

item.title: pour-rust-learning-refactor-audit
item.description: A learning-focused, prioritized inventory of refactor opportunities in the Pour codebase, mapped to The Rust Book chapters and rustlings exercise families. This is not a defect list. The codebase is at v1.0.0 and structurally sound; everything here is a teaching opportunity, not a bug. Sequencing. Findings are tagged beginner (Book Ch.1–10), intermediate (Ch.11–17), advanced (Ch.18–20). Pull early findings while Joseph is reading early chapters; let later ones wait. Effort. tiny (single function), small (single file), medium (cross-module), large (architectural). For a learner, tiny/small refactors are the strongest pedagogical units. Pragmatic-leave entries. The "Leave it alone" section is just as important as the refactor list. Show those examples so Joseph builds taste about when not to apply a pattern. ADR-006 is load-bearing. Config::edit, JsonStore<T>, and the 800-LOC ceiling are the v1.0.0 lock-in floor; do not propose refactors that break those — instead use them as case studies for why those shapes exist. No code changes during a lesson without Joseph's lead. The point of this codebase as a learning vehicle is that Joseph drives the typing. These are calibration points — patterns Joseph has already internalized. Don't lecture about them; reinforce with "you already do this in X" pointers. Zero unsafe. Zero macro_rules!. Across all 77 source files. The project does not lean on either escape hatch — there is no accidental unsafe to clean up. ? operator is the default. The majority of fallible code paths use ? cleanly — only 4 .expect() sites in src/**/*.rs total (config.rs:1257,1881,2232, transport/api.rs:83, idempotency.rs, submit/write_step.rs, submit/autocreate_step.rs), and only 39 .unwrap() sites — most of which are the deferred-borrow pattern app.form_state.as_mut().unwrap() after an is_some() guard. Typed errors over stringly-typed. ConfigError (src/config.rs:327), TransportReadError (src/transport/mod.rs:18), ReorderError (src/data/presets.rs:21), AxisError (src/data/preset_tree.rs:34) are all proper enum-based domain errors with Display/Error impls. This is Ch.9 done right. Option/Result combinator chains are used cleanly in many places, e.g. src/config.rs:471-475 chaining get/and_then/as_str/map. let-else for early returns is used pervasively (src/data/presets.rs:130-136, src/data/field_presets.rs:92-97, src/tui/loop_.rs handlers). Idiomatic 2024-edition Rust. Custom Display on enums for human output rather than relying on Debug (ConfigError, TransportReadError, TransportMode). The Config::edit closure-callback pattern (src/config_edit.rs:25) is genuinely sophisticated — it captures a transactional invariant in a single sanctioned API. This is closure-as-function-parameter at its best. PhantomData<fn() -> T> in JsonStore<T> (src/data/json_store.rs:35) is the correct phantom variance for a marker that should be covariant-and-not-Send-only-because-of-T. Many learners write PhantomData<T> without thinking; this one is intentional. Arc<Mutex<…>> is reserved for actual shared mutation (only AppState.presets, IdempotencyCache.inner, and IdempotencyCache itself). Most of the codebase uses ordinary &mut — no premature reaching for interior mutability. Newtype-ish constraint via pub(crate) mod. lib.rs already distinguishes a public surface from a crate-internal one (src/lib.rs:4-5). That instinct is correct — Slice 17 is just the formalization. Findings are grouped by Rust Book chapter / topic. Each has location, current snippet, alternative sketch, rationale, and tags. Location: src/config.rs:2216 (expect("current node must be in path when a cycle is detected")); src/transport/api.rs:84 (context("failed to build reqwest client...") — caller still propagates, this one is fine, but contrast with the others); src/server/handlers/submit/write_step.rs and submit/autocreate_step.rs (each has one .expect). Current shape: // src/config.rs:2213 let cycle_start = path .iter() .position(|&n| n == current) .expect("current node must be in path when a cycle is detected"); Idiomatic alternative. When an invariant is genuinely guaranteed by prior code in the same function, the expect message is OK in itself, but the Rust idiom for "guaranteed by prior code" is to refactor so the invariant is type-encoded — e.g. if let Some(pos) = path.iter().position(...) with the cycle-extraction logic inside the if let. Or, push the position call into a helper that returns Option<Cycle> and match on it. The Phase 6 hardening notes (pour-v1-decomposition.md §Hardening #6) flag these as "programming-by-coincidence" — the invariant lives only in the comment, not in the types. Why it matters. Joseph's existing expect sites are correct today but fragile to future edits: anyone moving the cycle-detection branch could turn the expect into a panic. This is the canonical "Ch.9 turn panics into typed errors" lesson. Pragmatic-leave note. Do not propose collapsing these to plain unwrap(). Either leave the expect (with a // SAFETY: comment as Joseph's project standards already prescribe) or convert to a typed return. Don't lose the explicit message. Difficulty: intermediate — Effort: tiny. Book link: Ch.9 §"To panic! or Not to panic!"; rustlings error_handling/. Location: 22 sites across the codebase, concentrated in src/tui/loop_.rs (5), src/config.rs (4), src/data/history.rs (3), src/data/history_legacy.rs (2), src/data/history_summary.rs (1), src/data/json_store.rs (1). Current shape: // src/data/history.rs:142 let _ = write_summary(&summary_path(&self.path), &self.summary); // src/config.rs:493 let _ = Self::write_atomic(config_path, &new_content); // src/data/json_store.rs:107 let _ = std::fs::remove_file(&tmp_path); Idiomatic alternative. Wrap with a tiny helper that names the intent — e.g. fn ignore_summary_write_error(r: io::Result<()>) or a small IgnoreErr extension trait — so the discard is typed as "best-effort". Or, route the swallowed error into App.deferred_stderr / app.set_status_warning so it's at least surfaced. Phase 8 of the decomposition plan (pour-v1-decomposition.md §Phase 8) notes this is a known UX gap. Why it matters. Each let _ = is a tiny decision: "I don't need to handle this." When that decision is correct, it's correct. The lesson is to develop taste about which 22 sites should stay let _ = and which should funnel through a structured error sink. Some of these (orphan tmp cleanup) are genuinely correct as-is. Others (history summary failures) are silent partial failures. Pragmatic-leave note. The // SAFETY: comments at src/data/history.rs:80, 141, 161 are the right pattern — the write succeeded; the cache write is best-effort. Don't refactor those. Difficulty: beginner-to-intermediate — Effort: small. Book link: Ch.9; rustlings error_handling/errors4. Location: src/config.rs:574 and src/config.rs:637 (secrets.toml read-and-merge); src/output/template.rs escape_nonspecifier_percent has none, but the cargo API call sites in src/transport/api.rs swallow body-read failures with resp.text().await.unwrap_or_default() at api.rs:134, 168, 193, 293, 337, 365. Current shape: // src/config.rs:571-574 let mut doc: DocumentMut = std::fs::read_to_string(&path) .ok() .and_then(|c| c.parse::<DocumentMut>().ok()) .unwrap_or_default(); This is correct if missing-file or parse-error means "start with empty doc"; but it also masks "permission denied" and "disk full" the same way. Idiomatic alternative. Match on io::Error::kind() and only default on ErrorKind::NotFound; propagate other I/O errors. The pattern is exactly what transport/fs.rs::read_file already does (fs.rs:386-394). Why it matters. Demonstrates the spectrum of Option collapse: ok() is convenient but throws away error kind. Result::map_err lets you keep the discriminator while reshaping the value. Pragmatic-leave note. The JsonStore::load use at json_store.rs:57 is consciously documented as "missing-or-parse-fail → default" and matches existing call-site behavior. Don't change that one without changing all three callers' contracts. Difficulty: intermediate — Effort: small per site. Book link: Ch.9 §"Where the ? Operator Can Be Used". Location: src/transport/fs.rs mixes anyhow::Result (most public methods, e.g. create_file:89, append_to_file:111) with std::result::Result<String, TransportReadError> (read_file:378). Current shape: create_file returns anyhow::Result<()> and uses anyhow::bail!("FS: file already exists: {}", ...). Callers then string-match (or rather, hopefully don't) on the error. read_file is the new typed shape. Idiomatic alternative. Define a TransportWriteError (or extend TransportReadError to a unified TransportError with NotFound, AlreadyExists, IoError, Validation variants). Use thiserror or hand-rolled Display+Error (Joseph already does the hand-rolled pattern at src/transport/mod.rs:27). Why it matters. Right now the API caller (e.g. autocreate.rs:174) cannot distinguish "file already exists" (a benign retry condition) from "permission denied" without parsing the Display string. This is exactly the lesson Joseph has already learned for read_file; the next pass extends it to writes. Pragmatic-leave note. anyhow is great for application code; this is library code. The boundary between "anyhow OK" and "typed error required" is one of the harder Ch.9 lessons — well worth a session. Difficulty: intermediate — Effort: medium (cross-module, all callers update). Book link: Ch.9 §"Defining Custom Error Types"; rustlings error_handling/errors5. Location: 299 .clone() calls across 46 files. The hot spots are src/tui/loop_.rs (39), src/server/dto/mapping.rs (36), src/app.rs (27), src/tui/configure/key/vault.rs (20), src/tui/configure/key/mod.rs (16), src/config_updates.rs (16), src/tui/form/mod.rs (14), src/server/handlers/submit/autocreate_step.rs (14). Current shape (representative): // src/tui/loop_.rs:506 let module_key = match app.module_keys.get(app.selected_module) { Some(k) => k.clone(), None => return, }; This pattern repeats ~21 times in loop_.rs alone — clone the module key out of app so a later &mut app borrow doesn't conflict. Idiomatic alternative. Split-borrow helper functions taking &str for the key plus disjoint &mut references to the specific App fields they touch — e.g. instead of handle_save_preset(app, ...) taking &mut App, take (&mut Presets, &mut Option<FormState>, &str) separately. Or, use Cow<'_, str> for the key when the function might borrow or own. For the genuinely cross-borrow cases (which most of these are), the clone is forced by NLL — they would need Polonius-style flow-sensitive borrowing which Rust doesn't have yet. Why it matters. Joseph's clone count is not high for a project this size — many clones are forced by the borrow checker. The lesson is to recognize which clones are unavoidable (most of these) versus which are habit (e.g. module_key.to_string() followed by &module_key — no clone needed if you keep the &str). src/tui/loop_.rs:822-823 (state.module_key.clone(); state.level.clone()) is a good example: the level.clone() is needed because match-then-mut, but module_key.clone() could potentially be &str if the call sites are restructured. Pragmatic-leave note. Do not chase clone count down for its own sake. A clone of a 16-byte String once per keystroke is invisible. The lesson is to see the clone, not to eliminate it. Difficulty: intermediate — Effort: small per site, medium cumulative. Book link: Ch.4 §"References and Borrowing", Ch.10 §"Lifetime Elision"; rustlings move_semantics/. Location: src/data/presets.rs:115 (set(&mut self, module_key: &str, entry: PresetEntry)) takes entry: PresetEntry by value but calls entry.name.clone() to do the find — well-formed; but src/app.rs:451-477 App::new(config: Config, transport: Transport, history: History, presets: Presets, field_presets: FieldPresets) takes everything by value, which is correct here (App owns them). Compare: src/data/preset_tree.rs:44 pub fn build(presets: &[PresetEntry], axes: &[String]) — already &[String], idiomatic. But many _updates.rs builders take &[ConfigSetting] then immediately setting.value.clone() — could those take Vec<ConfigSetting> and consume? Current shape: // src/config_updates.rs:15-89 pub fn build_module_updates(settings: &[ConfigSetting]) -> ModuleUpdates { // ... for setting in settings { match setting.key.as_str() { "path" => path = Some(setting.value.clone()), ... } } } Every match arm clones from a &ConfigSetting. If the caller passed Vec<ConfigSetting> and the function consumed it, the clones disappear — but the call sites usually want to keep the settings vec. Idiomatic alternative. Two paths: (a) accept Vec<ConfigSetting> by value; the call sites clone the vec themselves before calling (which is just moving the clone, not eliminating it — but makes it visible at the call site). (b) Stay with &[ConfigSetting]; this is the right answer because the caller usually does want to keep the settings vec for re-rendering. Why it matters. This is the teaching moment for Ch.4: a clone has to live somewhere. Pushing it to the caller doesn't reduce work; it just makes the cost visible. Sometimes that's the right move. Pragmatic-leave note. &str is already the default in this codebase — most string params are correctly borrowed. Don't go on a parameter-type sweep. Difficulty: beginner — Effort: tiny. Book link: Ch.4 §"The String Type" / "Slices"; rustlings strings/. Location: src/transport/api.rs:382-387: fn encode_vault_path(vault_path: &str) -> String { vault_path .split('/') .map(|segment| utf8_percent_encode(segment, PATH_SEGMENT).to_string()) .collect::<Vec<_>>() .join("/") } The collect::<Vec<_>>().join("/") allocates a Vec<String> just to immediately throw it away. Idiomatic alternative. Itertools::join for iterators (would add a dependency, not worth it), or use String::with_capacity and a manual loop, or use std::iter::Iterator::reduce. The zero-extra-alloc option: vault_path .split('/') .enumerate() .fold(String::new(), |mut acc, (i, seg)| { if i > 0 { acc.push('/'); } acc.extend(utf8_percent_encode(seg, PATH_SEGMENT)); acc }) Why it matters. The collect::<Vec>().join pattern is a common performance pothole. For a hot path it matters; for encode_vault_path called once per request it doesn't. The lesson is the taxonomy: when is the Vec worth eliminating? Pragmatic-leave note. Do not chase this in cold paths. Most .collect() calls in this codebase are correct. Difficulty: intermediate — Effort: tiny. Book link: Ch.13 §"Iterators"; rustlings iterators/. Location: src/output/template.rs:88 substitute_keys returns String even when no substitutions occurred. src/autocreate.rs:62 collapse_dashes always allocates even when input has no consecutive dashes. Current shape: // src/autocreate.rs:62 fn collapse_dashes(s: &str) -> String { let mut result = String::with_capacity(s.len()); // ... always allocates ... } Idiomatic alternative. Return Cow<'_, str>; if the input has no consecutive dashes, return Cow::Borrowed(s). This is the "famous example" of Cow — easy to teach, immediate payoff. Why it matters. Cow is one of the trickiest stdlib types for learners. collapse_dashes is a 15-line function with a clear borrow-vs-own decision — perfect teaching material. Pragmatic-leave note. This is genuinely a micro-optimization. It's a pedagogical opportunity, not a real performance win in this app. Difficulty: intermediate — Effort: tiny. Book link: Ch.15 §"Smart Pointers" (Cow is in std::borrow); rustlings does not cover Cow directly — this is a "go read the std::borrow docs" moment. Location: Most loops in this codebase are already iterator-chained appropriately. The hand-rolled ones are concentrated in: src/output/frontmatter.rs:60-64 (manual line-building), src/init.rs:18-34 (escape_toml_string char loop with control-char branch — fine, not iteratorable), src/transport/api.rs:382 (already iterator). Current shape (output/frontmatter.rs:58-64): if *list && value.contains(", ") { let items: Vec<&str> = value.split(", ").collect(); lines.push(format!("{key}:")); for item in items { let formatted = format_scalar(item); lines.push(format!(" - {formatted}")); } } Idiomatic alternative. Extend with an iterator chain: if *list && value.contains(", ") { lines.push(format!("{key}:")); lines.extend( value.split(", ").map(|item| format!(" - {}", format_scalar(item))) ); } Why it matters. This is one of the cleanest "before/after" pairs in the codebase. Use it as the canonical Ch.13 lesson example. Pragmatic-leave note. The manual for loops in output/template.rs:130-135 (prev_dash state machine) are explicitly state-machine logic and should NOT be iterator-fied. Iterator::scan exists but the manual form is easier to read. Difficulty: beginner — Effort: tiny. Book link: Ch.13 §"Processing a Series of Items with Iterators"; rustlings iterators/iterators4, iterators5. Location: src/config.rs:2554-2569 (show_when both/neither check), src/output/mod.rs:189-191 (composite (Some(subs), Some(rows)) destructure — already idiomatic). Current shape: // src/config.rs:2554 match (&sw.equals, &sw.one_of) { (Some(_), Some(_)) => { errors.push(...); } (None, None) => { errors.push(...); } _ => {} } This is already idiomatic — I'm including it as a positive example. Compare: // src/data/preset_tree.rs:144-152 nodes.sort_by(|a, b| match (a, b) { (TreeNode::Branch { axis_value: av, .. }, TreeNode::Branch { axis_value: bv, .. }) => av.cmp(bv), (TreeNode::Branch { .. }, TreeNode::Leaf { .. }) => std::cmp::Ordering::Less, (TreeNode::Leaf { .. }, TreeNode::Branch { .. }) => std::cmp::Ordering::Greater, (TreeNode::Leaf { .. }, TreeNode::Leaf { .. }) => std::cmp::Ordering::Equal, }); Also already great — destructuring with .. for the don't-care fields. Idiomatic alternative. None — these are the model. Use them as reference points when teaching Ch.18. Why it matters. Worth showing Joseph these are the gold-standard for tuple-pattern matching, so he doesn't second-guess his existing habits. Difficulty: beginner — Effort: N/A (no change recommended). Book link: Ch.18 §"Pattern Syntax". Location: Pervasive. src/main.rs:24-27, src/config.rs:1536-1540, src/tui/loop_.rs:104-107, 484-498, 750-790, etc. Current shape: // src/main.rs:24 if let Some(ref t) = template && !t.exists() { eprintln!("pour init: template not found: {}", t.display()); process::exit(1); } Idiomatic alternative. None — this is the 2024-edition idiom and Joseph uses it correctly. Worth flagging as a positive: pre-2024, this required nested if lets. The Mentor should note this when Joseph reads chapters that predate let-chains. Why it matters. Joseph is already Rust-2024 fluent here. The Book (most editions floating around) shows older patterns. Calibrate expectations. Difficulty: N/A — Effort: N/A. Book link: Ch.18 + edition-2024 release notes. Location: src/visibility.rs:44-53 does this idiomatically already (filter_map). src/data/preset_tree.rs:171-183 (validate_axes) uses filter_map correctly. Counter-example with room for cleanup: src/init.rs:262-268: for entry in entries.flatten() { let path = entry.path(); if path.is_dir() && path.join(".obsidian").is_dir() && !vaults.contains(&path) { vaults.push(path); } } Idiomatic alternative. This loop is fine as-is. The entries.flatten() already collapses Result<DirEntry, _> into successful entries. Pushing into a Vec inside an entries.flatten().filter(...).for_each(|p| vaults.push(p)) is no cleaner. Why it matters. Lesson: not every loop should be a chain. Joseph's instinct here is right. Difficulty: beginner — Effort: N/A (leave alone). Book link: Ch.13. Location: src/config.rs:241-323 defines ModuleUpdates, VaultUpdates, FieldUpdates, SubFieldUpdates — every "remove the key" field uses Option<Option<T>>: pub display_name: Option<Option<String>>, semantics: None = leave unchanged, Some(None) = remove, Some(Some(v)) = set. Current shape: Documented in comments at src/config.rs:248-249 and elsewhere. Used by ~32 mutator methods. Functionally correct. Idiomatic alternative. A three-variant enum: enum FieldChange<T> { Leave, Remove, Set(T), } Used as pub display_name: FieldChange<String>. Compile-checked match ergonomics; impossible to confuse Some(Some(v)) with Some(None). Why it matters. This is a textbook enum-driven state machine lesson (Ch.6 + Ch.17 trait objects vs enums). The current Option<Option<T>> works but every read site is a small puzzle for the reader. Pragmatic-leave note. DO NOT casually propose this refactor. ADR-006 explicitly froze the *Updates shape at v1.0.0 to avoid caller churn. The 32 facade methods would all churn. This is a teaching example — show Joseph the alternative, discuss the v2 cost, do not implement until v1.1+ if ever. Difficulty: intermediate (concept) / advanced (migration) — Effort: large. Book link: Ch.6 §"Defining an Enum"; Ch.17 §"Object-Oriented Programming Features". Location: src/app.rs:296 SettingKind enum. Current shape: Already a clean enum with Toggle(Vec<String>), QuickSelect(Vec<(char, String)>), etc. — payload-carrying variants for type-driven dispatch. Idiomatic alternative. None — this is the model. Use as a positive example when teaching Ch.6. Difficulty: N/A — Effort: N/A. Location: src/transport/fs.rs:151 append_under_heading(..., shallow: bool) and the matching API caller. src/data/presets.rs:146 reorder(..., direction: i32) (worse: a bool would say "two states"; i32 implies "any number" but only +1, -1 are valid). Current shape: pub fn reorder(&mut self, module_key: &str, preset_name: &str, direction: i32) { let new_idx = match direction { d if d > 0 => { ... } d if d < 0 => { ... } _ => return, // direction == 0, no-op }; } Idiomatic alternative. pub enum ReorderDirection { Up, Down } pub fn reorder(&mut self, module_key: &str, preset_name: &str, direction: ReorderDirection) { ... } Joseph already has MoveDirection at src/tui/dashboard.rs:14. Consolidate. Why it matters. "Stringly typed booleans" is one of the cheapest type-system wins. The 0-direction case in reorder is an unreachable state encoded in the type system. Pragmatic-leave note. shallow: bool is acceptable — there really are only two states and the parameter name is descriptive at the call site. The direction: i32 is not — there are 2³² values for "two states". Difficulty: beginner — Effort: small (Vec of call sites is bounded). Book link: Ch.6 §"The Option Enum"; "Make Illegal States Unrepresentable" — popular Rust talk reference. Location: src/data/json_store.rs:35. Current shape: PhantomData<fn() -> T> (not PhantomData<T>). Why it's the right choice. PhantomData<T> would give the wrapper the auto-trait properties of T (e.g. Send only if T: Send) which is wrong here — JsonStore only contains a PathBuf, so it should always be Send + Sync regardless of T. fn() -> T is the right marker for "I produce Ts but don't store one." Difficulty: advanced (concept). Worth a Mentor session — this is exactly the kind of subtle thing Joseph's writing already gets right but might not realize why. Book link: Ch.20 §"Advanced Types"; PhantomData is in std::marker, rustnomicon §"PhantomData". Location: src/lib.rs:1-13 — currently mixes pub mod and pub(crate) mod. Slice 17 (pour-v1-decomposition.md §Slice 17) is the explicit fix and is already complete on this branch (config_edit and config_updates are pub(crate)). Current shape: post-Slice-17, the surface is mostly correct. Remaining pub mod candidates worth reviewing: pub mod data (does every external integration test really need every nested item? data/preset_tree's public surface has no external consumers). Idiomatic alternative. Audit each pub mod against actual usage in tests/*.rs (per Slice-17's mechanism). Demote anything not externally needed. Why it matters. Module visibility is one of the most-skimmed Book chapters. Joseph already does this thoughtfully — Slice 17 is the ratified lesson. Use the diff between pre- and post-Slice-17 as teaching material. Pragmatic-leave note. ADR-006 makes some pub items contractual: Config::edit is pub, JsonStore<T> is pub, transport::atomic::atomic_replace is pub. These are not refactor candidates. Difficulty: intermediate — Effort: small. Book link: Ch.7 §"Paths for Referring to an Item in the Module Tree". Location: src/tui/mod.rs:9 (pub use loop_::{fetch_dynamic_options, run_loop};), src/tui/configure/mod.rs:84-97, src/server/mod.rs:8-13, src/data/history.rs:15 (pub use super::history_summary::HistorySummary;). Current shape: Idiomatic. The re-exports decouple the external name (pour::tui::run_loop) from the internal location (pour::tui::loop_::run_loop). Joseph already does this consistently. Idiomatic alternative. None — this is the model. Why it matters. pub use is a Ch.7 technique many learners miss. Use Joseph's existing examples to teach it. Difficulty: intermediate (concept) — Effort: N/A. Book link: Ch.7 §"Re-exporting Names with pub use". Location: Mixed across the codebase. src/tui/form/mod.rs is ~520 LOC and re-declares pub mod overlays; — uses the module/mod.rs style. src/data/mod.rs does the same. Meanwhile src/transport/mod.rs is 184 LOC and acts as the module body itself (no separate file). Current shape: Both styles coexist; both are valid Rust 2018+. Idiomatic alternative. The Rust community is split here; the modern preference is module.rs + module/... (i.e. drop the mod.rs filename) but module/mod.rs is also fine and what Joseph consistently uses. Why it matters. The Book uses both styles. Joseph picked one and stuck with it — that's the right answer. Don't refactor. Pragmatic-leave note. Don't suggest switching styles. The Mentor should show the alternative and explain it's preference, not refactor. Difficulty: beginner — Effort: N/A. Book link: Ch.7 §"Separating Modules into Different Files". Location: src/server/dto/mapping.rs:66-114 defines impl From<&ShowWhen> for ShowWhenDto, impl From<&SubFieldConfig> for SubFieldDto, impl From<&FieldConfig> for FieldDto. Current shape: Textbook. Lets call sites write f.show_when.as_ref().map(ShowWhenDto::from) — clean. Idiomatic alternative. None. Why it matters. From/Into is the most-misused trait pair for learners. Joseph's &Type → Dto pattern is exactly right when the source is borrowed and the destination is owned. Use as the positive example for Ch.10's traits chapter. Difficulty: intermediate (concept) — Effort: N/A. Book link: Ch.10 §"Defining Shared Behavior with Traits"; the std::convert docs. Location: src/config.rs:172 FieldType enum; DEVIATIONS.md C, "FieldType enum frozen at v1.0.0 — trait migration is v2 work". Current shape: Frozen enum. match exhaustive at every dispatch site (e.g. src/config.rs:1145-1152, 1454-1461). Idiomatic alternative. A trait FieldType { fn render_input(...); fn validate(...); fn write_output(...); } would be the textbook Ch.17 trait-object refactor. Explicitly out of scope for v1. Why it matters. This is one of the most pedagogically valuable decisions in the codebase: Joseph chose to keep an enum instead of splitting it into a trait. Trait-object thinking is a common over-application; the enum is correct here because (a) the variant set is closed by design, (b) exhaustive match is a useful safety net, (c) traits would force Box<dyn FieldType> allocations. Pragmatic-leave note. Use this as a Ch.17 lesson on "trait-object vs enum trade-offs". Refactoring Pour to a trait is precisely the wrong move. Difficulty: advanced (concept) — Effort: large (out of scope). Book link: Ch.17 §"Using Trait Objects"; ADR-006; pour-design-spec.md §4. Location: src/data/cache.rs:17 derive(Default), src/data/presets.rs:42 derive(Default), src/server/idempotency.rs:185 impl Default for IdempotencyCache (hand-rolled because Mutex<Inner> doesn't auto-derive sensibly). Current shape: Already correct. Auto-derive when possible; hand-roll when not. Idiomatic alternative. None. Why it matters. Lesson: derive(Default) is the default, until you need more. Joseph already gets this. Difficulty: beginner — Effort: N/A. Book link: Ch.5 §"Adding Useful Functionality with Derived Traits"; Ch.10. Location: src/server/mod.rs:62-75 AppState: pub struct AppState { pub transport_mode: TransportMode, pub token: String, pub config: Arc<Config>, // Arc, no Mutex (read-only after startup) pub transport: Arc<Transport>, // Arc, no Mutex (immutable) pub idempotency: Arc<IdempotencyCache>, // Arc, internal Mutex (struct does its own locking) pub presets: Arc<Mutex<Presets>>, // Arc<Mutex>, mutable shared state } Current shape: Each field uses the minimal synchronization primitive needed. config is Arc because it's read-only (no Mutex cost). idempotency puts the Mutex inside the struct (encapsulated). presets exposes the Mutex (handler-side await discipline). Idiomatic alternative. None. Why it matters. This is textbook Ch.16 done well — three different shared-state shapes in one struct, each chosen with reason. Use as the canonical Ch.16 example for Mentor lessons. Difficulty: advanced — Effort: N/A. Book link: Ch.16 §"Shared-State Concurrency"; Ch.15. Location: Search confirms zero Rc< in src/. Why it matters. Many learners reach for Rc<T> prematurely. Joseph doesn't — single-owner state stays as &mut/& borrows. This is the right instinct. Difficulty: beginner — Effort: N/A. Location: src/tui/loop_.rs:204-211 (Serve action handoff). Current shape: Spawns a Ctrl+C signal task, sends on a oneshot when fired, server's with_graceful_shutdown awaits the oneshot. Idiomatic alternative. None — this is exactly the tokio pattern for "register signal handler, signal cleanup future, drain on signal". Joseph implemented it correctly with all the documented edge cases (signal-handler-install-fails fallback at line 207-210). Why it matters. Async shutdown is a notorious footgun. This is the gold-standard shape for it. Use as a teaching reference when Joseph hits the async-book. Difficulty: advanced — Effort: N/A. Book link: Async book §"Graceful Shutdown"; tokio docs. Location: No tokio::select! macros in src/. Why it matters. select! is the most-overused tokio macro for learners. Joseph reaches for tokio::time::timeout(...) (loop_.rs:279) instead, which is the simpler and more correct tool when you really want "this future, but with a deadline." Use as a calibration point. Difficulty: advanced — Effort: N/A. Location: src/transport/mod.rs:77-87. Current shape: pub async fn connect(config: &Config) -> Self { if let (Some(port), Some(api_key)) = (...) && let Ok(client) = ApiClient::new(...) && client.check_connection().await { return Transport::Api(client); } let base_path = std::path::PathBuf::from(&config.vault.base_path); Transport::Fs(FsWriter::new(base_path)) } The function is async because of the check_connection().await call; the Fs branch is fully synchronous but inherits the async signature. Idiomatic alternative. This is correct. The alternative — a blocking connect_blocking or tokio::task::spawn_blocking for the fs branch — is worse: the API connection check has a 5-second timeout, and if you're going to wait up to 5s for the connection probe anyway, sync vs async makes no real difference; making it async means callers don't have to know which transport will win. Why it matters. Lesson: "should this be async?" is harder than "is it doing I/O?". Joseph chose the right answer for the right reason — the polymorphism over which transport wins is the controlling factor. Difficulty: intermediate — Effort: N/A. Location: All 51 test files in tests/ mirror src/ (per CLAUDE.md and Joseph's feedback_test_structure memory). Why it matters. This is enforced project policy. Don't suggest inline #[cfg(test)] mod tests — Joseph has explicit feedback on this. The Book often shows inline tests as the default; calibrate the lesson against this project's convention. Difficulty: beginner — Effort: N/A. Book link: Ch.11 §"How to Write Tests"; the contradiction between the Book's example and Pour's policy is itself a useful talking point. Location: tests/util_atomic.rs (every test), tests/data/..., most tests/transport/.... Why it matters. Test isolation via tempdir() + POUR_HOME env guard is exactly the right pattern. Use as a reference for Ch.11 testing chapters. Difficulty: intermediate — Effort: N/A. Location: Per the decomposition plan, "30 cases pinning render_path and render_append_template. Captured 8 intentional divergences." Why it matters. Snapshot tests pin observable behavior, not internal shape. Joseph already has the discipline; the convention is hand-rolled assertions instead of insta::assert_snapshot!. Both are valid; calibrate. Difficulty: intermediate — Effort: N/A (decomposition explicitly defers insta to post-tag). Book link: Ch.11; rustlings doesn't cover snapshot testing. Location: tests/config.rs:171 assert!(result.is_err()) over #[should_panic(expected = "...")]. Why it matters. #[should_panic] is the wrong tool for "this call returns Err"; Joseph correctly uses it only for genuine panic paths. Use as a calibration point — it's a Ch.11 distinction many learners blur. Difficulty: beginner — Effort: N/A. Book link: Ch.11 §"Checking for Panics with should_panic". Location: src/data/cache.rs:62, src/data/history.rs:269-271, src/data/presets.rs:116-122, src/data/field_presets.rs:81-87. Snippet: // src/data/history.rs:269-271 *counts.entry(entry.module_key.clone()).or_insert(0) += 1; Why it matters. entry().or_insert() is the canonical "increment-or-init" pattern; Joseph uses it correctly. Calibration. Difficulty: intermediate — Effort: N/A. Book link: Ch.8 §"Storing Keys with Associated Values in Hash Maps". Location: src/tui/loop_.rs:494, 760, 785. Snippet: field.options.get_or_insert_with(Vec::new).push(value.to_string()); Why it matters. get_or_insert_with(Vec::new) over get_or_insert(Vec::new()) — the closure form avoids allocating the default when not needed. Subtle, well-applied. Calibration. Difficulty: intermediate — Effort: N/A. Location: saturating_sub, saturating_add etc. in src/tui/... for layout math (form/mod.rs, dashboard.rs, summary.rs). Sample: src/tui/dashboard.rs:30-32: let week_start = today - chrono::Duration::days(weekday as i64); ... and many saturating_sub for Rect arithmetic. Why it matters. usize underflow panics. saturating_sub is the right tool. Joseph already uses it consistently. Calibration — many learners use - and learn the hard way. Difficulty: beginner — Effort: N/A. Location: Pervasive in src/tui/form/key/mod.rs:80-138, src/tui/form/key/text.rs, src/init.rs:18-34. The whole cursor-position story (per Phase 6 Hardening #3) is char-indexed. Why it matters. This is a hard-won lesson — the project had emoji/CJK panics before Phase 6 hardening. Joseph now uses chars().count() for length and char_indices().nth(idx) for byte conversion. Use as the canonical "byte-vs-char index" Ch.8 lesson. Difficulty: intermediate — Effort: N/A. Book link: Ch.8 §"Storing UTF-8 Encoded Text with Strings". Location: Pervasive across the codebase. Sample: src/output/template.rs:308: format!("{dir}{}", sanitize_filename_chars(filename)) Why it matters. Rust 1.58+ lets you reference variables directly in format strings. Joseph uses both styles, mostly the new one. Worth flagging as the modern idiom for any new code. Difficulty: beginner — Effort: tiny. Book link: N/A — this is post-Book material; just a 1.58 release note. Location: Config::from_toml (parse), Config::load (load+validate), App::new (constructor), Cache::load_from/Cache::load, Transport::connect (async constructor), IdempotencyCache::new, Presets::empty/Presets::load/Presets::load_from. Current shape: All correct per Rust API guidelines: new = primary constructor from_X = conversion from another shape (TOML string) with_X = could be used for builder-style options (not used here) load/load_from = side-effecting I/O constructor connect = async network constructor empty = explicit zero-state for tests Why it matters. Joseph's naming is unusually consistent. Calibration. Difficulty: beginner — Effort: N/A. Book link: Rust API Guidelines (not the Book): C-CONV. Location: No *Builder types in src/. Reasoning: most config shapes are deserialized from TOML, not constructed in Rust code. The *Updates structs are a builder-ish shape — partial-update patterns — but they don't pretend to be full builders. Why it matters. Builders are the Ch.5/Ch.10 hammer-and-nail problem. Joseph correctly avoided them where they don't fit. Lesson: "the builder pattern is for cases where construction has many optional parameters AND the caller is in Rust." Pour's config is in TOML; serde does the work. Difficulty: intermediate — Effort: N/A. Location: Confirmed by grep. Why it matters. Many learners reach for macro_rules! to dedupe similar code. Joseph has notably similar code — the 32 mutator methods on Config, the 4 *_updates builders — and did not reach for macros. This was the right call. Macros add a layer of indirection that makes errors harder to read; the duplication here is repetitive but readable. Pragmatic-leave note. Resist any temptation to suggest macro_rules! for the *_updates.rs builders or *_on_disk methods. They look duplicated; macroizing them would obscure the logic and make adding a 33rd field (or a new variant) harder, not easier. Difficulty: advanced — Effort: N/A. Book link: Ch.19 §"Macros". For Mentor: when Joseph asks "could I clean this up with X?", these are the cases where the answer is "yes you could, but don't". The 15 *_on_disk mutators in src/config.rs. They look duplicated; they aren't. Each one navigates to a different doc location and applies different rules. ADR-006 explicitly froze their signatures at v1.0.0 — refactoring is a v1.1+ concern. The 4 build_*_updates functions in src/config_updates.rs. Same reasoning — looks repetitive but each handles a different schema slice. Config::edit closure callback. Don't replace it with a "transaction guard" struct (RAII). The closure is more readable and makes the edit boundary explicit. ADR-006 Pattern 1. JsonStore<T> generic with migration hook. Don't try to make it more clever (e.g. Trait JsonMigratable). The closure-based migration is the right amount of polymorphism. ADR-006 Pattern 2. FieldType as a closed enum (D.2). Trait migration is v2 work per pour-design-spec.md §4. atomic_replace is one line (src/transport/atomic.rs:26-28). Don't add a "atomic write builder" or extract a fancier API. The one-line version is the API; the comment is the documentation. The 22 let _ = ... sites are not all bugs (A.2). Some are the right answer (orphan tmp cleanup; cache-write-on-success-path failures). Build taste before refactoring. The duplicate splice_under_heading logic in transport/api.rs:393-458 and transport/fs.rs:151-264. Per the decomposition plan, "splice_under_heading extraction — not actually duplicated (assessment claim was stale)" — the two functions diverge in subtle ways (different file-read paths). Don't refactor without re-reading both side-by-side. The ConfigSetting enum-driven settings UI (src/app.rs:296-310). Don't replace Vec<ConfigSetting> with a struct-of-fields — the list-driven shape is what makes the configure screen renderable uniformly. stringly-typed direction: i32 in Presets::reorder is flagged as a refactor opportunity (D.3). It is also the kind of refactor that's not worth doing in isolation — wait until Joseph is working in data/presets.rs for another reason and bundle it. A recommended Mentor sequence as Joseph progresses through The Rust Book. Each entry pairs a Book chapter with one Pour finding that the chapter unlocks. Don't pull from "what Joseph already does well" as a refactor target — those are calibrators, not work items.For rustlings: the highest-payoff exercise families to push Joseph through are iterators/, error_handling/, traits/, and lifetimes/. The codebase already correctly uses iterators and traits; rustlings will reinforce mechanics and Joseph won't be confused by patterns the Book hasn't covered yet.These came up during audit and Mentor should clarify them with Joseph before making teaching decisions, since they shape which refactors are appropriate. Is .expect("…verified above") a project-standards-approved pattern? A.1 cites the Phase 6 Hardening #6 entry that flagged these as "programming-by-coincidence", but pour-project-standards.md is ?? (untracked) — does the standards doc explicitly bless expect with // SAFETY: comments, or is the policy "use ? everywhere"? Will the v1.1 Option<Option<T>> → enum migration (D.1) actually happen, or is it a forever-deferred footnote? ADR-006 mentions demoting facades to pub(crate) in v1.1 but says nothing about the *Updates shape itself. Is transport::Transport::connect async-by-design or async-by-accident? H.3's reasoning assumes the polymorphism is the real driver; if Joseph remembers it as "I just wanted to call check_connection().await," that's worth knowing. For learning purposes, does Joseph want to keep anyhow at the library boundary, or is A.4 (typed TransportError) on the table for v1.x? This determines whether A.4 is a "lesson with refactor" or "lesson, no refactor." The *_on_disk mutators are explicitly frozen at v1.0.0 per ADR-006. Will future enums (e.g. a 33rd FieldUpdates field) be added by extending the struct, or is there a higher-level rewrite planned (e.g. JSON Patch-style PATCH operations)? Affects whether D.1's FieldChange<T> enum is "tomorrow's enum migration" or "never." Pour is a remarkably idiomatic Rust codebase for a self-taught project at v1.0.0. The structural-debt items have already been captured in DEVIATIONS.md and the v1-decomposition plan; the items in this audit are almost entirely teaching material rather than fixing material. That is itself the highest-value calibration: Joseph's instincts are good; the gap is mostly vocabulary for what he's already doing.When in doubt, lead a session by recognizing what Joseph already does in his own code, then introduce the Book's name for the pattern. The opposite direction — "the Book says X, here's a place we should apply X" — is the wrong shape for this learner. He is past that stage.
